Microsoft Excel Beginner Handbook

By Naomi Ajah · Edition 1, October 2026

How to Use This Handbook

This handbook takes you from zero to confident, everyday Excel in two parts. Part 1: Foundations (Chapters 1 to 7) covers the Excel window, navigation, data entry, sorting, filtering and a guided practical. Part 2: Analysis Tools (Chapters 8 to 17) adds formulas, functions, lookups, error fixing, validation, charts, PivotTables, printing and a capstone project.

All instructions apply to Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021. Older versions work the same way for almost everything here.

Each chapter opens with why the topic matters, then gives the steps or shortcuts you need, a business example, and hands-on practice. Keep Excel open while you read and try every step. Everyone makes mistakes in Excel, including experienced analysts, so watch for the Common mistake notes: they will save you hours.

Companion page: the Excel Handbook Lab is an interactive partner to this handbook, with chapter quizzes, a sortable practice sheet using the Zenith data, a live formula lab and shortcut flashcards. Open it in a second tab, read a chapter here, then practise there.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Microsoft Excel

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 1 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Excel is a spreadsheet application: software that stores data in a grid of rows and columns and calculates results automatically. Change one number and every formula, chart and summary that depends on it updates instantly.

Why it matters. Everything else in this handbook rests on three ideas: the grid, the cell address and the workbook. Learn them today and the rest will feel natural.

Common mistake: treating the file and a sheet as the same thing. The workbook is the file, and the sheets are the pages inside it.

1.1 The Grid

  • Rows run left to right and are numbered 1, 2, 3...

  • Columns run top to bottom and are lettered A, B, C...

  • A cell is the box where a row and column meet. Its address is the column letter plus the row number: the cell in column C, row 5 is C5.

Every formula you write will refer to cells by address, so this idea underpins everything that follows.

1.2 Why Excel Matters to a Data Analyst

  1. Raw data usually arrives in Excel. Accounting systems, CRMs, HR platforms and point-of-sale tools all export to .xlsx or .csv.

  2. It cleans and prepares data. Removing duplicates, fixing dates, standardising text and filling gaps often takes most of an analyst's time.

  3. It calculates automatically. Totals, averages, growth rates and lookups update the moment data changes.

  4. It visualises. Charts turn numbers into something a manager can read in seconds.

  5. Everyone uses it. You can send an Excel file to almost any colleague or client and they can open it.

  6. It is a foundation. Power BI, SQL and Python all use the same ideas: rows, columns, data types, sorting, filtering and aggregation.

1.3 Where Excel Is Used

DepartmentTypical Excel work
FinanceBudgets, cash-flow models, month-end reports, variance analysis
HRStaff registers, payroll preparation, leave tracking, headcount
SalesPerformance tracking, pipeline lists, commissions, target vs actual
MarketingCampaign tracking, ROI analysis, email and social metrics
OperationsInventory levels, supplier orders, delivery schedules
Customer serviceTicket logs, resolution times, satisfaction scores

Business example: A sales manager receives weekly figures from five regional teams, combines them in one tracker, highlights reps below target, and sends a summary to leadership every Monday.

1.4 Strengths and Limits

Strengths: no coding needed, very flexible, over 450 built-in functions, instant recalculation, charts and PivotTables, and a universal file format.

Limits to know about:

  • A worksheet holds at most 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns. Very large datasets need SQL or Python.

  • Excel is not a database. It does not enforce data rules, so inconsistent or duplicate data can be entered freely.

  • Formula errors are easy to make and hard to spot. A professional-looking sheet can still hold wrong numbers, so always check your work.

  • Repetitive daily reports are better automated with Power Query or scripts.

1.5 Workbooks and Worksheets

A workbook is the Excel file itself (.xlsx, or .xlsm if it contains macros). A worksheet (sheet) is one grid-page inside it. Think of the workbook as a notebook and each worksheet as a page.

A typical analyst workbook might hold sheets named Raw_Data, Calculations, Summary and Charts. Keeping them in one file makes it easy to share, while each sheet stays focused on one job.

TaskHow
Add a sheetClick the + next to the tabs, or press Shift + F11
RenameDouble-click the tab, type the new name, press Enter
MoveDrag the tab left or right
CopyRight-click the tab, Move or Copy, tick Create a copy
Colour-codeRight-click the tab, Tab Color
DeleteRight-click the tab, Delete (this cannot be undone)
ProtectRight-click the tab, Protect Sheet

Best practice: Use short, descriptive names without spaces (Jan_Sales, not Sheet1). Back up a workbook before deleting sheets.

Chapter 1 Summary

  • Excel is a grid of cells, each with an address such as C5.

  • Analysts use it to clean, calculate, summarise and visualise data.

  • It has real limits: size, no data rules, and easy-to-miss formula errors.

  • A workbook is the file; worksheets are the pages inside it.

Practice: Chapter 1

  1. Create a new workbook. Rename Sheet1 to My_First_Sheet, add a second sheet named Practice_Data with the + button, and a third named Reference with Shift + F11.

  2. Give Reference a tab colour, then drag the sheets into the order Practice_Data, My_First_Sheet, Reference.

  3. Save the file as Chapter1_Practice.xlsx.

  4. In your own words, explain the difference between a workbook and a worksheet, and name two limits of Excel.

Chapter 2: The Excel Interface

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 2 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Before you work efficiently in any software, you need to know the name and purpose of what is on the screen. This chapter walks through the Excel window from top to bottom. Keep Excel open and find each element as you read.

Why it matters. You cannot use a button you cannot find. Knowing where everything lives saves minutes every day.

Common mistake: panicking when the Ribbon disappears. It is not deleted: press Ctrl + F1 to bring it back.

2.1 Map of the Window

ZoneWhereWhat is in it
TopVery topTitle Bar, Quick Access Toolbar
RibbonBelow the topTabs, groups and commands
ReferenceBelow the RibbonName Box, Formula Bar
GridCentreColumn and row headers, cells, active cell
BottomVery bottomSheet tabs, Status Bar, scroll bars, Zoom

Figure 2.1: The Excel window. Find each numbered part on your own screen as you read.

2.2 Title Bar

Shows the workbook name followed by "Excel", for example Monthly_Budget.xlsx - Excel. A new unsaved file shows "Book1".

Habit: When several workbooks are open, glance at the Title Bar before you type or delete anything. If you see "Book1", save at once with Ctrl + S.

2.3 Quick Access Toolbar (QAT)

A small toolbar in the top-left corner that keeps your most-used commands one click away, whatever tab is active. It starts with Save, Undo and Redo.

To add a command: right-click it anywhere on the Ribbon and choose Add to Quick Access Toolbar.

Useful additions for analysts: Paste Special, Freeze Panes, Filter, Remove Duplicates, Sort Ascending, Print Preview.

Shortcut: Press Alt, then the number shown on a QAT button, to run it without the mouse. Keep the QAT to your 6 to 8 most-used commands.

2.4 The Ribbon

The Ribbon is where nearly every command lives. It has three levels:

  • Tabs: Home, Insert, Page Layout, Formulas, Data, Review, View, Help.

  • Groups: named sections within a tab, such as Clipboard or Font.

  • Commands: the buttons and menus inside each group.

Things to know:

  • Contextual tabs appear only when you select a chart, table or picture (for example Table Design) and vanish when you click away.

  • Dialog Box Launcher: the tiny arrow at the bottom-right of a group opens the full dialog for that group.

  • Tooltips: hover over any command for two seconds to see what it does and its shortcut.

  • KeyTips: press Alt to show letter labels on every tab and command, then press the letters to use the Ribbon without a mouse.

  • Collapse and restore: Ctrl + F1 toggles the Ribbon. If it disappears, press Ctrl + F1 again. It has not been deleted.

2.5 File Tab and Backstage View

The File tab opens a full-screen area for actions on the file as a whole. Press Esc to leave it.

SectionUse it to
New / OpenStart from a template or open recent files
Save / Save AsCtrl + S saves; F12 opens Save As for a new name, location or format
PrintPreview and set up printing (Ctrl + P)
Share / ExportShare via OneDrive or email; export a fixed PDF
InfoProtect the workbook, inspect it for hidden personal data, recover unsaved versions
OptionsChange settings such as AutoSave, default font, Enter-key direction

Beginner trap: Ctrl + S overwrites the existing file with no warning. To keep the original and save a copy, use F12 first.

2.6 The Home Tab

The Home tab is where you spend most of your time. It has seven groups.

Clipboard

  • Cut (Ctrl + X), Copy (Ctrl + C), Paste (Ctrl + V).

  • Format Painter: copies the formatting of one cell to others. Double-click it to apply to several places, then press Esc.

  • Paste Special (Ctrl + Alt + V): paste only part of what you copied.

Paste Special optionPastesTypical use
ValuesResults only, no formulas or formattingSharing numbers without your formulas
FormatsFormatting onlyCopying a template's look
FormulasFormula text onlyMoving logic without changing formatting
TransposeRows become columns and vice versaFixing data that arrived sideways
Paste LinkA live link to the source cellSummary sheets that update automatically

Warning: Before sending a report externally, convert formulas that reference other sheets or files to plain values with Paste Special, then Values. Otherwise recipients may see reference errors.

Font

Font name and size, Bold (Ctrl + B), Italic (Ctrl + I), Underline (Ctrl + U), Borders, Fill Color and Font Color.

  • Sizes that work well: 10 to 11 pt for data, 12 to 14 pt for headers, 16 to 18 pt for report titles.

  • Use muted, professional colours. Bright, saturated fills tire the eye.

  • Use thin borders inside tables and heavier ones to separate sections. Ctrl + Shift + & adds an outside border.

Alignment

  • Horizontal: Left, Centre, Right. Excel left-aligns text and right-aligns numbers by default. A number that sits on the left is probably stored as text.

  • Vertical: Top, Middle, Bottom.

  • Wrap Text: breaks long text onto several lines inside the cell (Alt + H, W).

  • Indent: nudges content in to show hierarchy.

  • Merge and Centre: joins cells into one. Avoid it inside data tables because it breaks sorting, filtering and PivotTables. For a centred title, use Centre Across Selection instead: Ctrl + 1, Alignment tab, Horizontal dropdown.

Number

The most important rule: number formatting changes how a value looks, never what it is. A cell storing 0.75 can display as 0.75, 75% or 0.750, and formulas always use 0.75.

FormatValue 1500.5 shows asUse for
General1500.5Default
Number1,500.50Counts, quantities
CurrencyN1,500.50Money (symbol set by you)
AccountingN 1,500.50Money columns with aligned symbols and decimals
Short Date15/01/2024Dates in reports
Percentage150050.00%Rates. Excel multiplies the stored value by 100
Text1500.5 (left-aligned)Identifiers only. Text cells are ignored by SUM

  • Percent trap: typing 25 then clicking the % button gives 2500%. Type 0.25 first, or type 25% directly.

  • Increase / Decrease Decimal change only the display, not the stored value.

  • Shortcuts: Ctrl + Shift + $ (Currency), Ctrl + Shift + % (Percentage).

Styles

  • Conditional Formatting: colours, data bars or icons applied automatically by rule, and updated as values change. Options include Highlight Cells, Top/Bottom rules, Data Bars, Color Scales and Icon Sets.

  • Format as Table (Ctrl + T): converts a range into an Excel Table with filter arrows, banded rows, automatic expansion and column-name formulas. Tables are covered again in Chapters 6 and 7.

  • Cell Styles: ready-made formatting combinations.

Business example: A sales analyst applies a green-yellow-red colour scale to an "Achievement %" column for 25 reps. Managers see at a glance who is on target and who needs help.

Cells

  • Insert / Delete rows, columns or sheets. Select the same number of rows you want to insert first. Ctrl + Shift + + inserts and Ctrl + - deletes.

  • Format: row height, column width, AutoFit, hide and unhide, protect sheet, and Format Cells (Ctrl + 1).

  • AutoFit: double-click the right edge of a column header (or bottom edge of a row header).

Warning: Deleting a row or column that formulas depend on creates #REF! errors. Use Formulas, Trace Dependents to check first.

Editing

  • AutoSum (Alt + =): inserts a SUM formula. Its dropdown also offers Average, Count, Max and Min. Select several result cells first and one press fills them all.

  • Fill: Fill Down (Ctrl + D), Fill Right (Ctrl + R), Series, and Flash Fill (Ctrl + E).

  • Clear: Clear All, Clear Formats, Clear Contents, Clear Comments. The Delete key is Clear Contents, which is why a deleted cell can keep its colour.

  • Find and Select: Find (Ctrl + F), Replace (Ctrl + H), Go To (Ctrl + G) and Go To Special, covered in Chapter 3.

2.7 The Other Tabs at a Glance

TabWhat it is forKey items
InsertAdding objectsPivotTable, Table (Ctrl + T), Pictures, Shapes, Charts, Sparklines, Slicers, Hyperlink (Ctrl + K), Header and Footer
Page LayoutThemes and printingThemes, Margins, Orientation, Print Area, Print Titles (repeat header row on every page), Scale to Fit
FormulasCalculation toolsFunction Library (fx), Name Manager, Trace Precedents / Dependents, Show Formulas (Ctrl + `), Evaluate Formula, Calculation Options (F9 to recalculate)
DataImport, clean, sort, filterGet Data (Power Query), Sort, Filter, Advanced, Text to Columns, Remove Duplicates, Data Validation, Group, Subtotal
ReviewChecking and protectingSpelling (F7), Comments and Notes, Protect Sheet / Workbook
ViewDisplay settingsFreeze Panes, Zoom, Page Break Preview, New Window, Gridlines and Headings toggles

Chart choice guide:

ChartBest for
Column / BarComparing categories, such as revenue by region
LineTrends over time
Pie / DoughnutShare of a whole, with few categories
ScatterRelationship between two variables
ComboTwo measures together, such as sales bars with a margin line

Not sure which chart to use? Select your data and click Recommended Charts.

Freeze Panes deserves special mention. On the View tab, Freeze Top Row keeps your header row visible while you scroll a long dataset, so you never lose track of which column is which. Unfreeze Panes reverses it.

Named ranges let you write =SUM(MonthlySales) instead of =SUM(C2:C150). The formula explains itself, and if the range grows you update the name once.

2.8 Name Box and Formula Bar

Name Box (left of the Formula Bar) shows the active cell's address, and it is also an input field. Click it, type an address and press Enter to jump there instantly: A5847, or B2:K500 to select a large range. Its dropdown lists named ranges.

Formula Bar shows what is actually stored in the active cell. A cell may display 2,500 while the bar shows =SUM(B2:B50), or display N1,234.57 while the bar shows 1234.567.

  • Always check the Formula Bar before trusting a value in a workbook you did not build.

  • Edit from the bar by clicking in it. Enter confirms, Esc cancels. F2 edits in the cell.

  • Ctrl + Shift + U expands the bar for long formulas.

  • The fx button opens the Insert Function dialog, or, when a formula is selected, its Function Arguments dialog.

  • Ctrl + ` shows every formula on the sheet at once, which is a fast audit.

2.9 Rows, Columns, Cells, Active Cell and Ranges

Rows are numbered 1 to 1,048,576 and columns are lettered A to XFD (16,384). Click a header to select the whole row or column.

In a structured dataset, each row is one record and each column is one field. Row 1 holds column headings, row 2 is the first record, and so on.

A cell has four independent layers: its content, its format, an optional comment, and an optional name. Changing the format never changes the content, and clearing the content never removes the format.

  • If text is too long for a cell, it spills into empty neighbours or is hidden behind filled ones. It is still stored in full.

  • If a number is too wide, the cell shows ######. That is not an error. Widen the column.

The active cell is the one with the coloured border and the one that receives what you type. It appears in three places: the grid, the Name Box and the Formula Bar. Check the Name Box before typing in a large sheet.

Cell address = column letter + row number (C5, AA15). Letters are used for columns so that addresses are never ambiguous.

Reference types in formulas:

TypeExampleBehaviour when copied
RelativeA1Shifts with the formula
Absolute$A$1Never changes
Mixed$A1 or A$1Locks only the column or only the row

Press F4 while the cursor is on a reference to cycle through them.

Example: To show each region's share of total revenue held in B1, write =C2/$B$1 and copy it down. The $B$1 stays fixed while C2 moves to C3, C4 and so on.

A range is a group of cells: A1:A10 (a column), B2:D5 (a block), A:A (a whole column), 1:1 (a whole row), or A1:A10,C1:C10 (two separate areas). Ranges are the inputs to functions, for example =SUM(B2:B100), =AVERAGE(C2:C50), =COUNTIF(D2:D500,"Lagos").

2.10 Status Bar, Sheet Tabs, Scroll Bars and Zoom

Status Bar. The left side shows the mode (Ready, Enter, Edit, Point). The right side shows Average, Count, Numerical Count, Min, Max and Sum of whatever cells you select, with no formula needed. Right-click the bar to choose which statistics appear. Text cells are ignored by Sum and Average.

Sheet Tabs. Switch sheets by clicking tabs or with Ctrl + Page Down / Page Up. Right-click for Insert, Delete, Rename, Move or Copy, Tab Color, Hide and Unhide.

  • Avoid Select All Sheets unless you mean it. It puts Excel in Group mode, where every edit hits every sheet. Click a single tab to exit.

  • Professional layout: raw data on the left, calculations in the middle, outputs on the right. Name sheets clearly and colour-code by purpose. In a large workbook, add a Contents sheet first.

Scroll Bars. Scrolling moves your view, not the active cell. If you scroll to row 800 and type, the entry goes into the cell that is still active, not the one you can see. Click a cell first.

Zoom. The slider (bottom-right) ranges from 10% to 400% and only changes your screen. It never affects printing. Ctrl + mouse wheel zooms quickly, and View, Zoom to Selection fits a range to the window. Return to 100% before saving a file you will share.

Chapter 2 Summary

  • Every element on the screen has a defined job: Title Bar, QAT, Ribbon, Name Box, Formula Bar, grid, Status Bar, tabs and Zoom.

  • The Home tab covers clipboard, formatting, number formats, styles, cells and editing.

  • The Formula Bar shows what a cell really holds. Always check it.

  • Format changes appearance only. Content and format are independent.

  • Use relative, absolute and mixed references deliberately, and press F4 to switch.

Practice: Chapter 2

  1. Ribbon tour: click each tab and read its group names. Press Ctrl + F1 to collapse the Ribbon and again to restore it. Press Alt and watch the KeyTips.

  2. QAT: add Print Preview, then add Bold by right-clicking it, then remove Bold.

  3. Name Box: type Z500 and Enter, then A1, then B2:E10. Compare what the Name Box and Status Bar show.

  4. Formula Bar: type your name in A1 and the number 1000 in B1. Apply Currency to B1. Compare what the cell shows with what the Formula Bar shows, and note the alignment of each.

  5. Freeze Panes: type the headers Date, Salesperson, Region, Product, Units, Revenue in A1:F1. Bold them with a dark fill and white text. Click A2 and apply Freeze Top Row. Press Ctrl + Down to confirm the headers stay visible, then unfreeze.

  6. Status Bar: enter 100, 250, 75, 400, 125, 300, 225, 175, 350, 200 in A1:A10. Select them and record Average, Count and Sum. Select only A1:A5 and watch the values change.

  7. Zoom: use Ctrl + mouse wheel, then select A1:F10 and click Zoom to Selection, then reset to 100%.

Chapter 3: Navigation and Selection

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 3 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Navigation means moving the active cell, scrolling the view, selecting cells, and switching sheets. Real datasets run to thousands of rows, so mouse-only navigation is slow. A keyboard shortcut can take you from row 1 to row 15,000 in under a second, and a few shortcuts separate someone who finishes an analysis in an hour from someone who needs three.

Why it matters. A one-second shortcut replaces half a minute of scrolling. On a 5,000-row file it is the difference between finishing and giving up.

Common mistake: trusting Ctrl + Arrow to reach the end of your data. It stops at the first blank cell, so a gap can make the data look shorter than it is.

3.1 When to Use Which Method

Dataset sizeRowsApproach
SmallUnder 100Mouse is fine
Medium100 to 5,000Mix of mouse and keyboard. Ctrl + Arrow and the Name Box become important
Large5,000 and overKeyboard shortcuts are essential

Learn the shortcuts on small datasets first, where you can see what happens.

3.2 Mouse Navigation

  • Click a cell to make it active. Click and drag to select a range.

  • Shift + Click extends a selection from the active cell to the cell you click. It is more accurate than dragging for ranges longer than one screen.

  • Double-click a cell to edit it (same as F2).

  • Right-click for a context menu with Cut, Copy, Paste Special, Insert, Delete and Format Cells.

  • Mouse wheel scrolls the view. Ctrl + wheel zooms. Shift + wheel scrolls sideways.

Remember: scrolling moves the view, not the active cell. Click a cell after scrolling before you type.

3.3 Keyboard Navigation

Arrow keys move one cell at a time. Use them for fine adjustments.

Ctrl + Arrow jumps to the edge of a block of data. This is the most important navigation shortcut for analysts.

  • Click A2, press Ctrl + Down to reach the last filled cell in the column. The Name Box shows the row number, which tells you how many records you have.

  • Ctrl + Right finds the last column, Ctrl + Up and Ctrl + Left go back.

  • It stops at every blank cell, so check that key columns have no gaps before you rely on it.

Ctrl + Home goes to A1. Always press it before saving a file you will share so it opens at the top.

Ctrl + End goes to the last used cell on the sheet. If it lands far beyond your data (say row 100,000 for 500 rows of data), formatted but empty cells exist. Select those rows and columns, use Clear All, and save.

Page Down / Page Up move one screen at a time, which is ideal for scanning a dataset section by section. Alt + Page Down / Page Up move one screen right or left.

Tab and Enter are for data entry. Tab confirms and moves right, and when you finish a row and press Enter, Excel returns you to the column where you started. Shift + Tab and Shift + Enter move in the opposite directions. You can change the Enter direction in File, Options, Advanced.

Selecting with the keyboard:

  • Shift + Arrow extends the selection one cell at a time.

  • Ctrl + Shift + Arrow extends it to the end of the data. From the first Revenue cell, Ctrl + Shift + Down selects all 8,456 values in one keystroke.

3.4 Name Box and Go To

Click the Name Box, type where you want to go, and press Enter.

TypeResult
D4892Jumps to that cell
B2:F200Selects that range
B:BSelects column B
5:5Selects row 5
A1:A10,C1:C10Selects two separate areas
SalesDataJumps to a named range

Go To (Ctrl + G or F5) does the same in a dialog and remembers recent locations. Its main value is the Special button.

3.5 Go To Special

Go To Special selects every cell that matches a type, wherever it is. Open it with Ctrl + G, then Special.

OptionSelectsUse it to
BlanksEvery empty cellFind missing data in a column
ConstantsTyped-in valuesAudit where numbers are hard-coded
FormulasFormula cells (also Errors, Numbers)Review calculations or find all errors
Current RegionThe whole block around the active cellSelect a table without knowing its size
Visible Cells OnlyCells not hidden by a filter or hidingCopy filtered data without hidden rows

Visible Cells Only (Alt + ;) solves a common beginner problem. If you filter a list and copy it, Excel also copies the hidden rows. Select the filtered range, press Alt + ;, then copy and paste.

Fill blanks in one go: select the column, use Go To Special, Blanks, type a value such as MISSING, and press Ctrl + Enter to fill every selected blank.

3.6 Selecting Cells, Rows, Columns and Sheets

To selectDo this
One cellClick it, arrive with the keyboard, or use the Name Box
A rangeDrag, Shift + Click, Name Box, Shift + Arrow, or Ctrl + Shift + Arrow
A whole rowClick the row number, or Shift + Space
A whole columnClick the column letter, or Ctrl + Space
Several rows or columnsClick the first header, hold Shift for consecutive or Ctrl for separate ones
Separate areasSelect the first, hold Ctrl, select the others
Data region, then whole sheetCtrl + A once, then again. Or click the corner square above row 1

Example: To format Revenue, Cost and Profit columns at once, click the first column letter, hold Ctrl and click the other two. Apply Currency once.

Selecting several sheets. Click the first tab, hold Shift (consecutive) or Ctrl (separate), and click the others. The Title Bar shows [Group], and now anything you type or format is applied to every selected sheet.

Use it to format 12 identical monthly sheets in one go, then immediately click a single tab to leave Group mode. Forgetting this and continuing to work can overwrite data on sheets you never meant to touch.

3.7 Navigation Shortcut Reference

ShortcutAction
Ctrl + Down / Up / Right / LeftJump to the edge of the data block
Ctrl + Home / Ctrl + EndA1 / last used cell
Page Down / Page UpOne screen down / up
Alt + Page Down / UpOne screen right / left
Tab / Shift + TabConfirm and move right / left
Enter / Shift + EnterConfirm and move down / up
Shift + ArrowExtend selection by one cell
Ctrl + Shift + ArrowExtend selection to the end of the data
Ctrl + ASelect data region, then the whole sheet
Ctrl + Space / Shift + SpaceSelect column / row
Ctrl + G or F5Go To
Alt + ;Select visible cells only
Ctrl + Page Down / UpNext / previous sheet

Chapter 3 Summary

  • Mouse navigation suits small data. Keyboard navigation is essential for large data.

  • Ctrl + Arrow, Ctrl + Home/End and the Name Box are your fastest ways to move.

  • Ctrl + Shift + Arrow selects a whole column or row of data in one keystroke.

  • Go To Special finds blanks, errors, formulas and visible cells instantly.

  • Always leave Group mode straight after using it.

Practice: Chapter 3

  1. Set up data: create the headers Employee ID, Name, Department, Salary, Start Date, then enter 20 fictional employees (IDs 1001 to 1020, departments rotating between Sales, Finance, HR and Operations, salaries between 150000 and 500000).

  2. Ctrl + Arrow: from A1 press Ctrl + Down, Ctrl + Right, Ctrl + Up, Ctrl + Left, then Ctrl + Home and Ctrl + End. Write down each address and confirm it matches the data.

  3. Name Box: go to D10, then select A1:E20, then select D:D and read the Sum on the Status Bar.

  4. Selection: select row 1 and bold it. Select columns B and E together with Ctrl and italicise them. Select A1, C1 and E1 together and fill them yellow.

  5. Go To Special: clear C10, B5 and D15. Select A1:E20, press Ctrl + G, Special, Blanks, type MISSING and press Ctrl + Enter.

  6. Sheet group: add Sheet2 and Sheet3, group all three, type GROUPED ENTRY in A1, then click one tab to exit. Confirm it appears on all three sheets. Move between sheets with Ctrl + Page Down and Ctrl + Page Up.

  7. Speed run: from any cell, reach A1, then select A1:E20, then select column D, using only the keyboard. Repeat and try to beat your first time.

Chapter 4: Data Entry

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 4 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Every analysis starts with data, and poor entry habits cause problems that are painful to fix later: numbers stored as text that will not add up, dates that will not sort, hidden spaces that break lookups. This chapter covers how Excel reads what you type, how to enter each data type correctly, and how to keep data consistent.

Why it matters. Most "Excel problems" are really data-entry problems. Clean entry now saves hours of fixing later.

Common mistake: typing the N symbol or commas into an amount. Excel stores it as text and SUM ignores it. Type the plain number and format it afterwards.

4.1 Data Types and How Excel Stores Them

Excel works with text, numbers, currency, percentages, dates, times and logical values. Alignment is your fastest diagnostic: text sits left, numbers, dates and times sit right, and TRUE/FALSE sits in the centre.

TypeAlignmentStored asEnter it as
TextLeftCharactersNaomi Ajah, SKU-001, Lagos
NumberRightNumber (15 digits of precision)1500, 3.14, -250
CurrencyRightA number plus a display format50000, then apply Currency
PercentageRightA decimal0.75 or 75%
DateRightA serial number (1 Jan 2024 = 45292)15/01/2024
TimeRightA fraction of a day (noon = 0.5)09:30 or 14:45
LogicalCentreTRUE or FALSETRUE

Text

Anything Excel cannot read as a number, date or time is text, including product codes, names and identifiers.

  • Leading zeros. Typing 08012345678 drops the zero. Type '08012345678 with a leading apostrophe (invisible in the cell), or format the cell as Text first. Use this for phone numbers and ID numbers.

  • Numbers stored as text will not SUM, AVERAGE or sort numerically, and show a green triangle in the corner. Common causes: pasting from a website or PDF, leading spaces, or a Text-formatted column.

  • Inconsistent text. Lagos, lagos, LAGOS and Lagos (trailing space) count as different values and break filters, lookups and PivotTables. Clean with =TRIM(), =PROPER(), =UPPER() and =LOWER().

Business example: An HR analyst's VLOOKUP of employee IDs fails. The imported IDs are "E001 " with a trailing space. =TRIM() fixes the whole column. Invisible spaces are among the most common causes of lookup failures.

Numbers and Currency

  • Type numbers plainly: 1500000, not 1,500,000. Commas and currency symbols are formatting, applied afterwards.

  • Do not type the currency symbol. Typing N150,000 makes Excel store text. A SUM of a column of such entries returns zero. Type 150000, then apply a Currency or Accounting format.

  • If you inherit text amounts, use Text to Columns (Data tab) to strip the symbols and convert them, then reformat.

  • Keep one currency and one unit per column. Note "in thousands" in the header if it applies.

Percentages

Excel stores 75% as 0.75. Enter 0.75 or 75%. Never type 75 and then click the % button, which shows 7500%.

You typeStoredDisplaysVerdict
0.750.7575%Correct
75%0.7575%Correct
75, then % format757500%Wrong

Because percentages are decimals, =B2*C2 with 100000 and 15% correctly returns 15000.

Dates

Because dates are numbers, you can subtract two dates to get days between them, or add days to a date. Enter dates as DD/MM/YYYY with a four-digit year, such as 15/01/2024.

  • Check alignment. A right-aligned date is a real date. A left-aligned one is text and will not sort, filter or calculate correctly.

  • Mixed columns are the most dangerous problem. 15/01/2024 (a date) and 15-01-2024 (text) look alike, but a date filter will capture only some rows. Verify the whole column, and convert text dates with Text to Columns.

  • Avoid two-digit years, which can be read as the wrong century.

  • Ctrl + ; inserts today's date and Ctrl + Shift + ; the current time, as fixed values that do not update.

Time

Enter times with a colon: 09:30, 14:45, or 09:30 AM. Times are fractions of a day, so =B2-A2 gives elapsed time, and multiplying by 24 converts it to hours. Entering 930 without a colon will not work, and calculations that cross midnight need special handling.

Logical Values

TRUE and FALSE come from comparisons such as =A1>100. In arithmetic TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, so summing a column of them counts the TRUEs.

4.2 Entering Data

  1. Click the cell and type. The text appears in both the cell and the Formula Bar.

  2. Confirm with Enter (down), Tab (right) or an arrow key. Esc cancels.

Efficient entry:

  • Down a column: type, press Enter.

  • Across a row: type, press Tab. At the end of the row, Enter returns you to the first column of the next row.

  • Same value in many cells: select them (hold Ctrl for separate cells), type, then press Ctrl + Enter.

  • AutoComplete: as you type text, Excel suggests earlier entries from the same column. Press Enter to accept. It speeds up repeated categories and keeps spelling consistent.

  • Several sheets at once: group the sheets as in Chapter 3, type, then ungroup immediately.

4.3 Editing, Deleting, Copying and Moving

Editing

  • Replace the whole entry: select the cell and start typing.

  • Edit part of it: press F2, double-click, or click in the Formula Bar.

  • Undo / Redo: Ctrl + Z and Ctrl + Y. Undo history is lost when you save or close, and some actions (deleting a sheet) cannot be undone.

Deleting

OptionRemovesKeepsUse when
Delete key / Clear ContentsValues and formulasAll formattingRefreshing a template with new data
Clear FormatsFormattingContentStripping messy formatting
Clear AllEverythingThe empty cellYou want a completely blank cell

Copying and moving

  • Copy with Ctrl + C, then Ctrl + V. Dismiss the marching ants with Esc.

  • Paste Special (Ctrl + Alt + V) gives you control. Values: Ctrl + Alt + V, V, Enter. Formats: Ctrl + Alt + V, T, Enter. Transpose: Ctrl + Alt + V, E, Enter.

  • Cut and paste (Ctrl + X, Ctrl + V) moves data. Formulas adjust to the new location.

  • Drag and drop: hover on the selection border until the four-arrow cursor appears, then drag. Hold Ctrl to copy instead of move, or Shift to insert between existing cells rather than overwrite. If you drop in the wrong place, press Ctrl + Z straight away.

4.4 The Fill Handle and AutoFill

The Fill Handle is the small green square at the bottom-right corner of the active cell. Hover and the cursor becomes a thin black cross. Drag it to copy or extend a pattern.

Starting value(s)Dragging gives
1 and 2 (both selected)3, 4, 5...
5 and 10 (both selected)15, 20, 25...
January or JanFebruary, March... wrapping after December
MondayTuesday, Wednesday...
Quarter 1 or Week 1Quarter 2, Quarter 3...
A dateNext days. The AutoFill Options button switches to weekdays, months or years
=A1*B1=A2*B2, =A3*B3...

A single number is copied rather than extended. Select two to set the step.

Double-click the Fill Handle to fill a formula down to match the adjacent column. This applies a formula to 10,000 rows in a second. It stops at the first blank cell in the neighbouring column, so for data with gaps drag manually or select the range and press Ctrl + D.

For precise control use Home, Fill, Series, where you set the series type, step and stop value. A 60-month column header row takes seconds.

4.5 Flash Fill

Flash Fill (Ctrl + E) spots a pattern in what you type beside existing data and completes the rest of the column. No formula is needed.

  1. Type the desired result for the first row in the adjacent column.

  2. Start the second row. If a grey preview appears, press Enter to accept it. If not, press Ctrl + E.

SourceYou typeFlash Fill produces
Naomi AjahNaomiFirst names of every row
Naomi AjahAjahLast names of every row
AJAH, NAOMINaomi Ajah"First Last" format for every row
080123456780801-234-5678Same format for every row

Flash Fill gives static results that do not update if the source changes, so use it for one-off cleaning. Use formulas (LEFT, MID, TRIM, PROPER) when results must stay live. Always check the output, because ambiguous patterns can go wrong in some rows.

Business example: An HR analyst has 350 names as AJAH, NAOMI. She types the first two in "Naomi Ajah" form, Flash Fill previews the rest, and she presses Enter. It takes seconds instead of hours.

4.6 Data Consistency

Data can be accurate but inconsistent, and Excel treats Lagos, lagos and LAGOS as three different values. Consistency is what makes sorting, filtering, lookups and PivotTables reliable.

ProblemExampleFix
CapitalisationLagos / lagos / LAGOSPROPER, UPPER or LOWER
Extra spaces"Naomi "TRIM on the whole column
Mixed date formats15/01/2024, Jan 15, 15-01-24Text to Columns, then check right-alignment
Numbers as text"500" with a hidden spaceVALUE or Text to Columns
Variant namesHR, H.R., Human ResourcesOne standard name, enforced by a dropdown
Mixed unitsSome full, some in thousandsOne unit per column, stated in the header

Prevent it with Data Validation (Data tab, Data Tools). Restrict a cell to a dropdown list, a number range, a date range or a rule. For categories such as Department, Region or Status, a dropdown eliminates spelling and capitalisation variants completely.

Business example: An expense tracker completed by 15 staff produces "Travel", "travel", "Travelling", "Transport" and "Transport costs", so a PivotTable shows seven categories instead of one. Adding a dropdown of eight approved categories fixes every month that follows.

Chapter 4 Summary

  • Alignment tells you how Excel read an entry: text left, numbers and dates right.

  • Currency and percentage are number formats. Enter the plain number or decimal.

  • Enter dates as DD/MM/YYYY and confirm they right-align.

  • Ctrl + Enter, F2, the Fill Handle, Ctrl + E and Paste Special are your core entry tools.

  • Delete keeps formatting. Clear All removes everything.

  • Clean existing data with TRIM and PROPER. Prevent new problems with Data Validation.

Practice: Chapter 4

  1. Headers: in A1:F1 type Employee ID, Full Name, Department, Salary (NGN), Start Date, Status. Bold them with a navy fill and white text, then apply Freeze Top Row.

  2. Entry: add 10 employees. IDs as 'EMP001, Title Case names, departments from Sales, Finance, Operations and HR only, salaries of 150000 to 500000 with no symbols or commas, dates as DD/MM/YYYY, status Active or Inactive. Check the alignment of each column.

  3. Formats: apply Currency to the salary column, confirm the Formula Bar still shows plain numbers, compare with Accounting, then return to Currency.

  4. AutoFill: from H1 fill "January" down 12 cells, then 100 and 200 as a series, then "Quarter 1" down 3 cells. Enter today's date, drag it down 6 cells, and switch it to Fill Months.

  5. Flash Fill: type six full names in M1:M6. In N1 type the first name of the first person, start N2, and accept the preview or press Ctrl + E. Repeat for last names.

  6. Editing: edit B5 with F2, overwrite C7, delete D8:D10 and re-enter them (notice the formatting stays), then use Clear Formats on B3 and undo it.

  7. Consistency audit: type sales in C3, HR (with a trailing space) in C6 and AMARA JOHNSON in B8. Fix them with =TRIM() and =PROPER() in helper columns. How would you fix 500 such rows?

  8. Paste Special: copy A1:F11, paste to A15 as Values, undo, then as Formats, undo, then as Transpose.

Chapter 5: Sorting Data

Practise this chapter: sort the Zenith data on the Practice sheet, then take the Chapter 5 quiz.

Sorting reorders every row of a dataset by the values in one or more columns. It answers questions about ranking, chronology and grouping: top products by revenue, orders from oldest to newest, staff listed alphabetically by department.

Why it matters. Sorting answers "who is top?" in one click, and it makes patterns in your data visible.

Common mistake: sorting one column on its own. The other columns stay put and your records are scrambled with no warning, so always sort the whole table.

5.1 Prepare Before You Sort

  • Convert the data to an Excel Table (Ctrl + T) so Excel always knows where the data starts and ends.

  • Remove blank rows inside the data and avoid merged cells.

  • Make sure numbers and dates are real numbers and dates (right-aligned), not text.

  • Click inside the data, not on a blank cell outside it.

Warning: Always sort the whole table. If only one column is selected and Excel offers to sort just that column, choose Expand the selection. Otherwise one column is reordered while the others stay put, and your records are scrambled with no warning.

5.2 Quick Sort on One Column

Click any cell in the column, then use the Data tab:

Column typeAscending (A to Z)Descending (Z to A)
TextA to ZZ to A
NumbersSmallest to largestLargest to smallest
DatesOldest to newestNewest to oldest

You can also use the filter dropdown arrow on a Table header and choose a sort option.

5.3 Multi-Level Sort

Figure 5.1: The Sort dialog with two levels. Open it from Data, Sort.

Use it when one column has repeated values and you want a second column to order the ties.

  1. Click inside the data, then Data, Sort.

  2. Set the first level, for example Region, A to Z.

  3. Click Add Level and set the second, for example Revenue, Largest to Smallest.

  4. Click OK.

Order matters. Sorting by Region then Revenue groups orders by region and ranks them within each region. Reversing the levels would rank all orders by revenue first, and Region would only break ties between orders with identical revenue.

5.4 Other Sorts

  • By colour or icon: in the Sort dialog, change Sort On from Cell Values to Cell Color, Font Color or Icon.

  • Custom list: for non-alphabetical orders such as Low, Medium, High, choose Custom List under Order.

  • Undo: Ctrl + Z reverses a sort. Once you save and close, the old order is gone, so add a numbered ID column if you may need to restore the original order.

5.5 Sorting vs Filtering

SortingFiltering
EffectReorders every rowHides rows that do not match
DataPhysical order changesOrder unchanged, visibility changes
Use forRankings, chronology, groupingFocusing on a subset

You will usually use both: filter to the rows you want, then sort the result.

Chapter 5 Summary

  • Sort the whole table, never a single column in isolation.

  • Quick sort handles one column. Use the Sort dialog for several levels, and mind their order.

  • Sorting changes sequence. Filtering changes visibility.

Practice: Chapter 5

Using your Chapter 4 employee table:

  1. Sort by Salary largest to smallest. Who earns the most?

  2. Sort by Start Date oldest to newest.

  3. Sort by Department A to Z, then Salary largest to smallest.

  4. Undo each sort with Ctrl + Z after checking the result.

Chapter 6: Filtering Data

Practise this chapter: filter the Zenith data on the Practice sheet, then take the Chapter 6 quiz.

Filtering temporarily hides the rows that do not meet your criteria, leaving the original data intact. Hidden rows are not deleted, and their row numbers simply turn blue. The Status Bar tells you how many records remain, such as "23 of 1,847 records found". Filtering is how analysts turn a 50,000-row dataset into the 47 rows that answer a specific question.

Why it matters. Filtering is how you turn a huge table into the few rows that answer today's question.

Common mistake: reading a total off a filtered table. SUM still counts hidden rows. Use the Status Bar on the visible cells, or SUBTOTAL, when you want only what is showing.

Figure 6.1: Open the drop-down arrow on a header, untick Select All, and tick the values you want to keep.

Business questions filtering answers:

  • Sales: deals won last quarter by the top representative.

  • Finance: transactions above a threshold, for audit sampling.

  • HR: staff hired in the last 90 days who have not completed onboarding.

  • Customer service: tickets that are Open, Critical and Unassigned.

  • Marketing: campaigns with ROI above 300% in one region.

6.1 Prepare Your Data

Convert your data to an Excel Table first (click inside it, press Ctrl + T, tick "My table has headers"). Filter arrows appear automatically, the table grows as you add rows, and Excel always knows where the data ends.

Things that break filtering, so fix them first:

  • Blank rows inside the data.

  • Merged cells.

  • Duplicate or missing column headers.

  • Numbers or dates stored as text. Numeric and date filters will not work correctly on them.

6.2 Turning Filters On and Off

ActionHow
Toggle filter arrowsData, Filter, or Ctrl + Shift + L
Open the filter menu on a headerAlt + Down Arrow
Clear one column's filterHeader arrow, Clear Filter From "Column"
Clear all filtersData, Clear, or Alt + A + C
Reapply after data changesData, Reapply, or Ctrl + Alt + L
Advanced Filter dialogData, Advanced, or Alt + A + Q

Clearing a filter never deletes data. It just shows everything again.

6.3 The Filter Menu

Click a header arrow. You will see a Search box, a list of every unique value with checkboxes, (Select All), then Text, Number or Date Filters (depending on the column), and Filter by Color.

For checkbox filtering, untick (Select All) first, then tick the values you want.

Multiple filters use AND logic. Filtering Region = West, Sales Rep = Maria Lopez and Revenue > 10,000 shows only rows that satisfy all three. If the Status Bar reports "0 of 12,450 records", your criteria are too strict. Clear one.

6.4 Text, Number and Date Filters

Text Filters: Equals, Does Not Equal, Begins With, Ends With, Contains, Does Not Contain, and Custom Filter (two conditions joined by AND or OR).

Example: to find open tickets that mention "refund", filter Ticket Description with Contains refund, then filter Status with Does Not Equal Resolved.

Number Filters: Equals, Greater Than, Less Than, Between, Top 10 (switch Items to Percent for the top 10%), Above Average, Below Average, and Custom Filter.

Example: invoices over N50,000 this fiscal year. Filter Amount with Greater Than 50000, and Invoice Date with a Date Filter.

Date Filters: Today, This Week, This Month, This Quarter, Year to Date, Last Year, All Dates in the Period, Between, and more.

Example: staff with a work anniversary this month. Filter Hire Date with Date Filters, This Month, then sort by date.

Warning: Date filters only appear and work if the column holds real dates. If they are text, convert them first with the green warning triangle or Text to Columns.

6.5 Search Filter and Filter by Colour

Search box. In a column of 8,000 products, click the arrow, type battery and press Enter. Only matching items remain. You can combine it with other filters, such as Quantity less than 50.

Filter by colour or icon. Works with manual fills, font colours and Conditional Formatting icons. In a risk register, filter Risk Level by the red fill, then Status = Open, to get a focused action list for the steering committee.

6.6 Advanced Filter

The dropdown arrows cannot easily do OR logic across different columns, extract unique values, copy results to another place, or use formulas as criteria. Advanced Filter can.

  1. Create a criteria range above or beside your data. Its top row must be exact copies of your column headers.

  2. Put conditions beneath the headers. Conditions on the same row mean AND. Conditions on different rows mean OR.

  3. Click inside your data, then Data, Advanced.

  4. Choose Filter the list, in-place, or Copy to another location (and give a destination cell).

  5. Set the List range and Criteria range, then click OK.

Example: (Department = Sales AND Salary > 80000) OR (Department = Marketing AND Performance Score = Exceeds):

DepartmentSalaryPerformance Score
Sales>80000
MarketingExceeds

Copying to another location produces a clean report area and leaves your source data untouched.

6.7 Reapplying Filters

Filters do not update themselves when you edit, add or delete data. After changing the data, click Reapply or press Ctrl + Alt + L.

6.8 Copying Filtered Data

After filtering, select the visible range and press Alt + ; (Visible Cells Only), then copy and paste. Otherwise the hidden rows come along too.

6.9 Common Mistakes and Best Practices

Mistakes

  • Filtering without converting to a Table first.

  • Forgetting that filters across columns combine with AND.

  • Filtering columns that contain merged cells or text-formatted dates.

  • Not noticing an old filter still active on another column.

  • Clearing a filter and assuming data was deleted.

Best practices

  • Work inside a Table, and use the Search box before scrolling long lists.

  • Combine text, number, date and colour filters to answer complex questions.

  • Use Advanced Filter for OR logic or to extract results elsewhere.

  • For very complex criteria, add a helper column such as =IF(AND(...),"Include","Exclude") and filter on it.

  • Clear all filters before saving or sharing so the next person sees the full picture.

  • For recurring reports, consider Power Query, which can refresh automatically.

Chapter 6 Summary

  • Filtering hides rows and never deletes them.

  • Tables make filtering safe and dynamic.

  • Text, number, date, search and colour filters cover most needs. Several filters combine as AND.

  • Use Advanced Filter for OR logic and to copy results elsewhere.

  • Reapply filters after changing data, and clear them before sharing.

Practice: Chapter 6

  1. Checkbox filter: build a table with Date, Region, Sales Rep, Product Category, Units and Revenue (12 to 15 rows). Convert it to a Table. Filter to Region = West, then add Revenue greater than 5,000. Clear the filters.

  2. Text and number: filter Product Category with Contains Pro, then show the Top 5 by Revenue.

  3. Date: filter the Date column to Last Quarter, then sort the result by Revenue descending.

  4. Colour: apply Conditional Formatting to Revenue (green above average, red below), then filter by green.

  5. Advanced Filter: build a criteria range with two rows (Region = North in one, Revenue > 15000 in the other) and copy the matches to J2.

Chapter 7: Guided Practical Exercise

Practise this chapter: repeat the exercise on the Practice sheet, then take the Chapter 7 quiz.

This chapter ties Chapters 1 to 6 into one workflow: set up a workbook, enter a dataset, navigate it, format it, sort it and filter it to answer business questions. Allow 60 to 90 minutes, and save with Ctrl + S if you need a break. Answers are in Appendix B.

Why it matters. This is where the skills turn into a habit. You build a real workbook from a blank file, the way you will at work.

Common mistake: rushing the first two parts. One wrong date or one number stored as text early on will break every later step, so check alignment as you go.

7.1 The Scenario

You are a Data Analyst at Zenith Consumer Goods Limited, a Nigerian company distributing across Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano and Ibadan. The Head of Sales wants the Q1 2024 sales records (January to March) in a professional workbook for Monday's management meeting. She must be able to find sales by region, sales rep, product category and order status quickly.

7.3 Part 1: Set Up the Workbook

Step 1 — Save. Press Ctrl + N for a new workbook, then F12 and save it as Zenith_ConsumerGoods_Q1_Sales_2024.xlsx. Check that the Title Bar no longer says "Book1".

Step 2 — Sheets. Rename Sheet1 to Q1_Sales_Data (green tab). Add a sheet named Notes (grey tab). On Notes, type "Workbook Documentation" in A1, then in A3:B6 record Created by (your name), Date created, Purpose (Q1 2024 sales records for Zenith Consumer Goods Ltd) and Data source (manual entry from paper records).

Step 3 — Headers. On Q1_Sales_Data, type the ten headers from the table above in A1:J1, pressing Tab between them.

Step 4 — Format the header row. Select row 1 and apply Ctrl + B, fill colour hex 1F3864, white font colour and 11 pt. Use the Alignment group's Center button (note that Ctrl + E is Flash Fill in Excel, not centre). Set row height to 22.

Step 5 — Column widths. Right-click each column header, choose Column Width, and set A 12, B 14, C 18, D 16, E 20, F 24, G 12, H 16, I 16, J 14.

Step 6 — Freeze the header. Click A2, then View, Freeze Panes, Freeze Top Row.

Checkpoint: a navy header row with white bold text that stays visible when you scroll.

7.4 Part 2: Enter the Data

  1. Order IDs (A2:A31): type ORD-001 and continue to ORD-030. The hyphen makes Excel treat them as text, so no apostrophe is needed. You can enter the first few and AutoFill the rest, but check the result.

  2. Dates (B2:B31): enter as DD/MM/YYYY. Every date must right-align. If one left-aligns, retype it.

  3. Sales Rep, Region, Category, Product Name (C:F): type each entry once, then let AutoComplete help with repeats.

  4. Units and Unit Price (G, H): plain numbers. All must right-align.

  5. Revenue (I2): type =G2*H2, press Enter, and the result for ORD-001 should be 186000. Check that the Formula Bar shows the formula, not the number. Double-click the Fill Handle to fill down to I31. Click I5 and confirm it reads =G5*H5.

  6. Status (J2:J31): Completed, Pending or Cancelled.

  7. Number format: select H2:I31 and apply Comma Style (or Accounting with an N symbol via Ctrl + 1). Use the same format on both columns.

Checkpoint: Order IDs left-aligned, dates and numbers right-aligned, and no #VALUE! errors in column I.

7.5 Part 3: Table Formatting and Title

  1. Click inside the data and press Ctrl + T. Tick "My table has headers" and pick a blue banded style such as Table Style Medium 2. This adds filter arrows and alternating row colours.

  2. Right-click row 1, choose Insert, and type Zenith Consumer Goods Limited — Q1 2024 Sales Records in A1.

  3. Select A1:J1 and open Ctrl + 1, Alignment. Set Horizontal to Center Across Selection. This is used instead of Merge and Centre, which can interfere with the table and with sorting.

  4. Format the title: 14 pt, bold, font 1F3864, fill DEEAF1, row height 30.

  5. Select all columns A to J and double-click a column border to AutoFit.

  6. Press Ctrl + Home and save.

Your headers are now in row 2 and data in rows 3 to 32.

7.6 Part 4: Navigate the Dataset

  1. Click A3 and press Ctrl + Down. Which cell do you land on? Then press Ctrl + Right, Ctrl + Up, and Ctrl + Home.

  2. In the Name Box type I3:I32 and press Enter. Write down the Sum from the Status Bar. Then select C3:C32 and read the Count.

  3. Press Page Down and Page Up, then scroll with the mouse wheel and watch the frozen header stay in place.

7.7 Part 5: Sort the Data

Click inside the table for each sort and press Ctrl + Z to undo it before the next.

  1. By Order Date, oldest to newest. The Head of Sales wants a chronological view. Which order is first and which is last?

  2. By Revenue, largest to smallest. Write down the top three orders.

  3. By Sales Rep, A to Z. Count each rep's orders.

  4. Multi-level: Region A to Z, then Revenue largest to smallest (Data, Sort, Add Level). What is the highest-revenue Lagos order?

  5. Multi-level: Status A to Z, then Order Date oldest to newest. How many orders are Cancelled and which IDs?

7.8 Part 6: Filter the Data

Clear the filter after each task (Data, Clear). Select the visible Revenue cells and read the Status Bar Sum where asked.

  1. Lagos orders. How many are there, and what is the total revenue?

  2. Completed Electronics orders (two filters together). How many, which IDs, and what total revenue?

  3. February orders (expand the date list in the Order Date filter). How many, and what total revenue?

  4. Emeka Okafor's orders (use the Search box). How many, total revenue, and which regions?

  5. High-value orders: Revenue greater than 200,000 (Number Filters, Greater Than). How many, and which rep has the most?

  6. Cancelled orders. List Order ID, Sales Rep, Region, Product and Revenue on your Notes sheet.

7.9 Part 7: Quality Check

  • Ctrl + End lands on J32 (not far beyond).

  • I3 shows =G3*H3 and I32 shows =G32*H32 in the Formula Bar.

  • B3:B32 are real dates (right-aligned, Format Cells shows Date).

  • H and I share one number format.

  • No filter is active (no funnel icon in any header).

  • Press Ctrl + Home, save, close with Ctrl + W, reopen, and confirm it opens at A1 with everything intact.

7.10 Reflection Questions

  1. Why does right-alignment tell you a date is stored correctly, and what goes wrong with a column that mixes true dates and text dates?

  2. What would have happened to the formula in I5 if you had used =$G$2*$H$2?

  3. Why does the order of sort levels matter? What would Region-then-Revenue look like if reversed?

  4. Filtering Electronics and Completed together is an AND filter. How would you show Electronics OR Clothing?

  5. What extra improvements would make this workbook more useful for Monday's meeting?

Part 1 taught you to enter, find and organise data. Part 2 teaches you to make the data answer questions. Every example uses the 30-order workbook you built in Chapter 7, so keep that file open.

About the examples. Work on the sheet Q1_Sales_Data. With the title row you added, the headers are in row 2 and the 30 orders are in rows 3 to 32. The columns are:

ColumnHoldsColumnHolds
AOrder IDFProduct Name
BOrder DateGUnits Sold
CSales RepHUnit Price (NGN)
DRegionIRevenue (NGN)
EProduct CategoryJStatus

Type the practice formulas in empty cells to the right of the data (start at column L) so you never overwrite your orders.

Chapter 8: Formulas and Everyday Functions

Practise this chapter: type real formulas in the Formula lab, then take the Chapter 8 quiz.

Why it matters. A formula is what turns Excel from a place to store numbers into a tool that works with them. Once your totals are formulas, they update by themselves when the data changes. That is the habit that separates a spreadsheet user from an analyst.

8.1 What a Formula Is

A formula is an instruction that starts with an equals sign. Excel works out the answer and shows the result in the cell, while the Formula Bar keeps the instruction.

Figure 8.1: The parts of a formula, and the order in which Excel calculates.

Common mistake: forgetting the =. Typing SUM(I3:I32) without it just shows the text.

8.2 Operators and Order of Operations

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
+Add=G3+G432
-Subtract=G4-G38
*Multiply=G3*H3186,000
/Divide=I3/G315,500
^Power=G3^2144
&Join text=C3&" - "&D3Emeka Okafor - Lagos

Excel calculates brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. =2+3*4 gives 14, but =(2+3)*4 gives 20. When in doubt, add brackets.

8.3 Cell References

A formula should point at cells, not repeat numbers you typed. If you write =I3*0.05 the 5% is buried inside the formula. Put the rate in its own cell and refer to it, so you can change it once.

Figure 8.2: the relative reference B2 moves as you copy down, while the absolute reference $B$7 stays locked.

TypeLooks likeWhen copied
RelativeB2Shifts with the formula
Absolute$B$7Never changes
Mixed$B2 or B$2Locks only the column or only the row

Press F4 while the cursor is on a reference to cycle through the types.

Common mistake: copying a share-of-total formula down without locking the total. Row 2 works, row 3 divides by an empty cell and shows #DIV/0!.

8.4 AutoSum and the Core Functions

A function is a ready-made formula. Type =, the function name, an opening bracket, the range, and a closing bracket. AutoSum (Alt + =) writes =SUM(...) for you: click the cell under a column of numbers and press it.

FunctionWhat it doesExampleResult
SUMAdds numbers=SUM(I3:I32)6,888,900
AVERAGEMean of numbers=AVERAGE(I3:I32)229,630
MEDIANMiddle value=MEDIAN(I3:I32)189,000
COUNTCounts cells holding numbers=COUNT(G3:G32)30
COUNTACounts cells that are not empty=COUNTA(A3:A32)30
MAXLargest value=MAX(I3:I32)720,000
MINSmallest value=MIN(I3:I32)97,500
ROUNDRounds to a number of digits=ROUND(AVERAGE(I3:I32),-3)230,000

The average (229,630) is higher than the median (189,000) because a few very large orders pull the average up. When a dataset has big outliers, the median is often the fairer picture of a typical order.

ROUND with a negative number rounds to the left of the decimal point: -3 rounds to the nearest thousand. Rounding the formula changes the value, while number formatting only changes how it looks.

Tip: a function can contain another function, as in ROUND(AVERAGE(...),-3). Excel works from the inside out.

8.5 Writing Formulas the Easy Way

  1. Type = and the first letters of a function. A list of matching functions appears. Press Tab to pick one.

  2. After the bracket, drag across the range with the mouse or use Ctrl + Shift + Arrow. Excel writes the reference for you.

  3. Press Enter.

  4. To edit, press F2. Cells and ranges the formula uses are outlined in matching colours.

  5. To see every formula on the sheet, press Ctrl + Grave accent (the key above Tab).

8.6 Percentages and Growth

Share of total: =I3/SUM($I$3:$I$32), then format as a percentage. ORD-028 (720,000) is 10.5% of the 6,888,900 total.

Percentage change: =(New-Old)/Old. Monthly revenue was 2,357,500 in January, 2,375,000 in February and 2,156,400 in March. February grew 0.7% on January, and March fell 9.2% on February.

8.7 Automatic and Manual Calculation

By default Excel recalculates as soon as you change a number. On very large files people sometimes switch to manual calculation, and then results look stale. If numbers do not update, check Formulas, Calculation Options and press F9 to recalculate.

Chapter 8 Summary

  • Every formula starts with = and points at cells, not typed-in numbers.

  • Brackets control the order of calculation.

  • Lock a reference with a dollar sign (F4) when it must not move as you copy.

  • SUM, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, COUNT, COUNTA, MAX, MIN and ROUND cover most everyday needs.

  • Median protects you from outliers that distort the average.

Practice: Chapter 8

  1. In L2, find the total units sold.

  2. In L3, find the average units per order.

  3. In L4 and L5, find the largest and smallest revenue.

  4. In L6, find ORD-028's share of total revenue as a percentage with one decimal.

  5. In L7, find the percentage change in monthly revenue from February to March.

Answers are in Appendix D.

Chapter 9: Logic and Conditional Summaries

Practise this chapter: try the IF and SUMIFS missions in the Formula lab, then take the Chapter 9 quiz.

Why it matters. Managers rarely ask for "the total". They ask for the total for Lagos, the number of cancelled orders, or which orders need follow-up. Logic functions let a formula make a decision, and conditional summary functions add up or count only the rows that qualify.

9.1 The IF Function

IF asks a yes/no question and returns one answer if it is true and another if it is false.

=IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)

In a spare column (say K, with a header "Order Size") type this in K3 and fill down:

=IF(I3>=200000,"High","Standard")

ORD-001 (186,000) shows Standard and ORD-002 (360,000) shows High. Count the results with =COUNTIF(K3:K32,"High"): 12 of the 30 orders reach 200,000.

ComparisonMeaning
=Equal to
<>Not equal to
> and <Greater than, less than
>= and <=Greater than or equal, less than or equal

Text in a formula always goes inside double quotes, numbers do not.

Example: commission. Put a 5% rate in cell O1. Then =IF(J3="Completed",I3*$O$1,0) pays commission only on completed orders. Fill it down and add it up: the total commission is 243,720. Change O1 to 6% and every result updates.

9.2 AND, OR and Nested IF

NeedFormulaOrders matching
Both conditions true=IF(AND(D3="Lagos",J3="Completed"),"Yes","No")9
At least one true=IF(OR(J3="Pending",J3="Cancelled"),"Follow up","OK")8

To choose between three or more outcomes, put one IF inside another:

=IF(I3>=500000,"Large",IF(I3>=200000,"Medium","Small"))

This gives 2 Large, 10 Medium and 18 Small orders. Excel tests from left to right and stops at the first true condition, so list the biggest threshold first.

Common mistake: a nested IF where the brackets do not match. Count that every opening bracket has a closing one. Excel colours matching pairs as you type.

9.3 SUMIF, COUNTIF and AVERAGEIF

These add, count or average only the cells that meet one condition.

=SUMIF(range_to_check, condition, range_to_add)
=COUNTIF(range_to_check, condition)
=AVERAGEIF(range_to_check, condition, range_to_average)
QuestionFormulaResult
Lagos revenue=SUMIF(D3:D32,"Lagos",I3:I32)2,145,900
Cancelled orders=COUNTIF(J3:J32,"Cancelled")3
Average Lagos order=AVERAGEIF(D3:D32,"Lagos",I3:I32)214,590
Orders above 200,000=COUNTIF(I3:I32,">200000")11
Products with "Rice" in the name=COUNTIF(F3:F32,"*Rice*")2

When the condition is a comparison, write it inside quotes: ">200000". The asterisk is a wildcard that stands for any text, so "*Rice*" matches Premium Rice (25kg) and Rice (50kg). Matching ignores capital letters.

Better still, point the condition at a cell: =SUMIF(D3:D32,N2,I3:I32) with "Lagos" typed in N2. Change N2 to "Kano" and the answer changes with it.

9.4 Several Conditions: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS

Add an "S" to apply two or more conditions at once. Note that in SUMIFS the range to add comes first.

=SUMIFS(range_to_add, range1, condition1, range2, condition2)
QuestionFormulaResult
Completed Lagos revenue=SUMIFS(I3:I32,D3:D32,"Lagos",J3:J32,"Completed")1,977,900
Completed Electronics orders=COUNTIFS(E3:E32,"Electronics",J3:J32,"Completed")8
Pending Groceries revenue=SUMIFS(I3:I32,E3:E32,"Groceries",J3:J32,"Pending")955,000
February revenue=SUMIFS(I3:I32,B3:B32,">="&DATE(2024,2,1),B3:B32,"<="&DATE(2024,2,29))2,375,000

For a date range, join the comparison to a DATE with the & operator, as in the last row.

9.5 IFERROR: A Safety Net

IFERROR shows a friendly value when a formula would return an error.

=IFERROR(I3/G3,0) returns the unit price, or 0 if the units cell is empty or zero. Use it carefully: it hides all errors, including ones you should fix. Chapter 12 explains how to find the cause first.

Chapter 9 Summary

  • IF returns one result when a test is true and another when it is false.

  • AND and OR combine tests, and IF can be nested for several outcomes.

  • SUMIF, COUNTIF and AVERAGEIF work on one condition. The "S" versions take many.

  • Put conditions in cells so formulas can be reused.

Practice: Chapter 9

  1. How many orders are "High" (revenue of at least 200,000)?

  2. What is the total revenue of completed Kano orders?

  3. How many orders sold 30 units or more?

  4. What is the total revenue of those orders?

  5. What is the total revenue lost to cancelled orders?

Answers are in Appendix D.

Chapter 10: Text, Date and Time Functions

Practise this chapter: try text and date formulas in the Formula lab, then take the Chapter 10 quiz.

Why it matters. Real data is messy: names with extra spaces, codes that need splitting, dates you need to group by month. These functions clean and reshape data without retyping it.

10.1 Cleaning Text

FunctionDoesExampleResult
TRIMRemoves extra spaces=TRIM(" Lagos ")Lagos
UPPERAll capitals=UPPER(D3)LAGOS
LOWERAll lower case=LOWER(D3)lagos
PROPERCapital first letters=PROPER("AMARA EZE")Amara Eze
LENCounts characters=LEN(C3)12
SUBSTITUTESwaps text=SUBSTITUTE(F3," ","_")Bluetooth_Speaker

The usual cleaning recipe is =PROPER(TRIM(A2)). After cleaning, copy the helper column and use Paste Special, Values over the original, then delete the helper.

10.2 Extracting and Joining Text

FunctionDoesExampleResult
LEFTFirst characters=LEFT(A3,3)ORD
RIGHTLast characters=RIGHT(A3,3)001
MIDCharacters from the middle=MID(A3,5,3)001
FINDPosition of a character=FIND(" ",C3)6
& or TEXTJOINJoin text=C3&" ("&D3&")"Emeka Okafor (Lagos)

Combine them to split a full name. In row 3 the rep is Emeka Okafor and the first space is at position 6:

  • First name: =LEFT(C3,FIND(" ",C3)-1) gives Emeka.

  • Last name: =MID(C3,FIND(" ",C3)+1,50) gives Okafor.

For one-off jobs, Flash Fill (Ctrl + E, Chapter 4) is faster. Use formulas when the source data will keep changing.

=RIGHT(A3,3) returns the text "001". To turn it into the number 1, wrap it in VALUE: =VALUE(RIGHT(A3,3)).

Common mistake: assuming text-function results are numbers. They are text until you convert them, so they will not add up.

10.3 Working with Dates

Excel stores a date as a serial number (Chapter 4), so you can calculate with dates and pull parts out of them. Row 3 holds 05/01/2024.

FunctionDoesExampleResult
YEARThe year=YEAR(B3)2024
MONTHMonth number=MONTH(B3)1
DAYDay of month=DAY(B3)5
TEXTDate as words=TEXT(B3,"mmmm")January
TEXTWeekday name=TEXT(B3,"dddd")Friday
DATEBuild a date=DATE(2024,3,31)31/03/2024
EOMONTHLast day of a month=EOMONTH(B3,0)31/01/2024
TODAYToday's date=TODAY()Updates every day

A helper column of =TEXT(B3,"mmm") gives every order a month label, which is exactly what you need to group by month in a PivotTable (Chapter 15).

10.4 Calculating with Dates

QuestionFormulaResult
Days between first and last order=B32-B384
Complete months between them=DATEDIF(B3,B32,"m")2
Working days (Monday to Friday)=NETWORKDAYS(B3,B32)61
Date 30 days after an order=B3+3004/02/2024

Format a date-difference cell as General or Number. If it shows a date such as 24/03/1900, change the format. DATEDIF works but is hidden from Excel's function list, so type it in full.

TODAY() and NOW() recalculate every time the workbook opens. Use Ctrl + ; if you need a date that stays fixed.

Chapter 10 Summary

  • TRIM, PROPER, UPPER and LOWER clean text.

  • LEFT, RIGHT, MID and FIND split text, and & joins it.

  • YEAR, MONTH, DAY and TEXT pull parts out of dates.

  • Subtract dates for days, and use NETWORKDAYS for working days.

Practice: Chapter 10

  1. Write the first name of the rep on ORD-001.

  2. Write that rep's last name.

  3. Turn the order number in A3 into the number 1.

  4. Give the month name of ORD-020 (28/02/2024).

  5. How many days separate the first and last order?

  6. How many working days is that?

Answers are in Appendix D.

Chapter 11: Lookup Functions

Practise this chapter: try XLOOKUP in the Formula lab, then take the Chapter 11 quiz.

Why it matters. Data lives in more than one place: orders in one sheet, sales targets in another, prices in a third. A lookup finds a value in one table and brings the matching information into another, with no copying and pasting. It is one of the skills employers ask about most.

11.1 Set Up a Lookup Table

Add a new sheet named Targets and type this small table in A1:C7. Q1 targets are example figures for practice.

RepRegionQ1 Target (NGN)
Emeka OkaforLagos900,000
Naomi AjahAbuja750,000
Chidi NwosuPort Harcourt800,000
Funke AdelekeKano850,000
Amara EzeIbadan700,000
Bola AdesanyaLagos800,000

A good lookup table has one row per item, the key (here the rep name) is unique, and there are no merged cells or stray spaces.

11.2 XLOOKUP

Figure 11.1: XLOOKUP looks for a value, finds it in one column and returns the matching cell from another.

=XLOOKUP(what to find, where to look, what to return, if not found)

In a new column on Q1_Sales_Data (header "Rep Target"), enter in L3 and fill down:

=XLOOKUP(C3,Targets!$A$2:$A$7,Targets!$C$2:$C$7,"Not found")

ORD-001 belongs to Emeka Okafor, so L3 shows 900,000. The dollar signs lock the lookup table while the formula copies down. Targets! tells Excel the range sits on another sheet.

XLOOKUP is available in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 or newer. It can look to the left, it finds exact matches by default, and the fourth argument saves you from ugly errors.

11.3 VLOOKUP

VLOOKUP is the older function. You will meet it in many existing workbooks, and it works in every version.

=VLOOKUP(what to find, table, column number, FALSE)

=VLOOKUP(C3,Targets!$A$2:$C$7,3,FALSE) also returns 900,000 for ORD-001: it finds Emeka in the first column and returns the 3rd column of the table.

  • The lookup value must be in the first column of the table.

  • Always type FALSE for an exact match. Leaving it out or typing TRUE can silently return wrong answers.

  • The column number breaks if someone inserts a column in the table. XLOOKUP does not have this problem.

11.4 INDEX and MATCH

Before XLOOKUP, analysts combined two functions: MATCH finds the position and INDEX returns the value at that position.

=INDEX(Targets!$C$2:$C$7,MATCH(C3,Targets!$A$2:$A$7,0))

The 0 means exact match. This also returns 900,000, and works in every version of Excel.

11.5 Approximate Match: Banded Rates

Sometimes you want the band a number falls into, not an exact match. A commission scheme might pay 2% under 200,000, 3% from 200,000, and 5% from 500,000. On a sheet named Bands, type thresholds in A2:A4 (0, 200000, 500000) and rates in B2:B4 (2%, 3%, 5%).

=XLOOKUP(I3,Bands!$A$2:$A$4,Bands!$B$2:$B$4,,-1)

The last argument, -1, means "exact match or the next smaller value". ORD-001 (186,000) gets 2%, ORD-015 (385,000) gets 3%, and ORD-028 (720,000) gets 5%.

11.6 Putting Lookups to Work

Combine SUMIF (Chapter 9) with a lookup to compare each rep with target. On the Targets sheet, add D1 "Revenue" and E1 "Achievement":

  • D2: =SUMIF(Q1_Sales_Data!$C$3:$C$32,A2,Q1_Sales_Data!$I$3:$I$32)

  • E2: =D2/C2, formatted as a percentage

RepTargetRevenueAchievement
Emeka Okafor900,000961,400106.8%
Naomi Ajah750,000965,700128.8%
Chidi Nwosu800,0001,129,500141.2%
Funke Adeleke850,0001,822,800214.4%
Amara Eze700,000825,000117.9%
Bola Adesanya800,0001,184,500148.1%

Common mistakes with lookups: a trailing space in either table, so "Naomi Ajah " does not match "Naomi Ajah" (use TRIM, Chapter 10); a number stored as text in one table and a real number in the other; and forgetting to lock the table with dollar signs, so the range slides down as you copy.

Chapter 11 Summary

  • A lookup finds a value in one table and returns a related value from another.

  • Use XLOOKUP when you can, VLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH for compatibility.

  • Lock the lookup table with $, and always ask for an exact match unless you want a band.

  • A clean, unique key column makes lookups reliable.

Practice: Chapter 11

  2. Find Funke Adeleke's revenue and achievement.

  3. Which rep is the only one below 110% of target?

  4. What commission rate applies to ORD-015 (385,000) under the bands in 11.5?

  5. What does your XLOOKUP show for a rep called "Ngozi"?
