Chapter 12: Understanding and Fixing Errors

Practise this chapter: trigger and fix errors in the Formula lab, then take the Chapter 12 quiz.

Why it matters. An error message is Excel telling you exactly what is wrong. Beginners panic at the first #, but each one has a short list of causes. Learning them turns errors into clues, and the habit of checking your work is what makes you trusted with numbers.

12.1 The Error Messages

ErrorMeansTypical causeFix
######Cell too narrowWide number or dateWiden the column (not a true error)
#DIV/0!Division by zeroDividing by 0 or an empty cellCheck the divisor, or wrap with IFERROR
#N/AValue not availableA lookup found no matchCheck spelling and spaces, or give XLOOKUP a "not found" result
#NAME?Excel does not recognise textMisspelt function, or text without quotesCorrect the spelling or add quotes
#REF!Broken referenceA row, column or sheet the formula used was deletedUndo, or rewrite the reference
#VALUE!Wrong type of valueAdding text to a numberRemove text or convert it
#NUM!Invalid numberImpossible calculationCheck the inputs
#NULL!Bad rangeA missing comma or colonFix the range
#SPILL!Result has nowhere to goCells blocking a multi-cell resultClear the cells in the way

Examples from your workbook:

  • =I3/(G3-G3) returns #DIV/0!.

  • =SUMM(I3:I32) returns #NAME?, because the function is spelt wrongly.

  • =C3*2 returns #VALUE!, because C3 holds the name Emeka Okafor.

  • =VLOOKUP("Ngozi",Targets!$A$2:$C$7,3,FALSE) returns #N/A, because no rep has that name.

  • If =H3*G3 exists and you delete column H, the formula becomes #REF!.

12.2 Other Warning Signs

  • Green triangle in a cell corner: Excel suspects a problem, such as a number stored as text or a formula that differs from its neighbours. Click the warning icon to see why.

  • Circular reference warning: a formula refers to its own cell, directly or through others. Excel cannot finish the calculation. Find it under Formulas, Error Checking, Circular References.

  • Numbers that will not add up: often numbers stored as text. Check the alignment (Chapter 4) and use Text to Columns or VALUE to convert.

  • A formula that shows as text: the cell was formatted as Text before the formula was typed. Change the format to General, press F2, then Enter.

12.3 Auditing Tools

On the Formulas tab, the Formula Auditing group helps you trace a problem to its source:

  • Trace Precedents draws arrows from the cells a formula uses.

  • Trace Dependents shows which formulas use the selected cell. Use it before you delete anything.

  • Evaluate Formula steps through a long formula one calculation at a time.

  • Show Formulas (Ctrl + Grave accent) displays every formula on the sheet at once.

  • Error Checking moves through the errors on the sheet.

12.4 A Debugging Routine

  1. Read the error name and look up its cause in 12.1.

  2. Click the cell and read the formula in the Formula Bar.

  3. Check each cell it refers to: is it empty, text, or misspelt?

  4. Use Evaluate Formula on anything long.

  5. Fix the cause, then copy the corrected formula down the whole column.

  6. Only then consider IFERROR. It hides problems, so use it for expected situations, not to cover mistakes.

Check your own work. Compare totals two ways, for example the sum of the Revenue column against the sum of region totals. Both should equal 6,888,900. If they do not, something is wrong.

Chapter 12 Summary

  • Each error message points to a specific cause.

  • ###### only means the column is too narrow.

  • Use Trace Dependents before deleting, and Evaluate Formula for long formulas.

  • Fix the cause before using IFERROR.

Practice: Chapter 12

Name the error each formula returns:

  1. =SUMM(I3:I32)

  2. =C3*2

  3. =I3/(G3-G3)

  4. =H3*G3 after column H is deleted

  5. =VLOOKUP("Ngozi",Targets!$A$2:$C$7,3,FALSE)

Answers are in Appendix D.

Chapter 13: Data Validation and Conditional Formatting

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 13 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Why it matters. Validation stops bad data entering your sheet. Conditional formatting makes important data stand out the moment you open the file. Together they make a workbook that is both reliable and easy to read.

Figure 13.1: Left, a drop-down list created with Data Validation. Right, a colour scale applied with Conditional Formatting.

13.1 Data Validation

Select the cells, then Data, Data Validation. The Settings tab decides what is allowed.

AllowUse it forExample
ListA fixed set of choicesStatus: Completed, Pending, Cancelled
Whole numberCountsUnits Sold between 1 and 1000
DecimalAmountsUnit Price greater than 0
DateDate limitsOrder Date in 2024
Text lengthFixed-length codesOrder ID exactly 7 characters
CustomYour own ruleA formula that returns TRUE or FALSE

Build a drop-down for Status:

  1. Select J3:J32.

  2. Choose Data, Data Validation, and set Allow to List.

  3. In Source type Completed,Pending,Cancelled, with commas and no spaces.

  4. Open the Input Message tab to add a hint, and the Error Alert tab to choose a Stop message such as "Choose Completed, Pending or Cancelled".

  5. Click OK. Each cell now has a drop-down arrow.

For a longer list, type the items in a column on another sheet and select that range as the Source. The drop-down updates when you edit the list.

Find existing bad data: choose Data Validation, Circle Invalid Data and Excel circles every value that breaks the rule. Remember that validation does not check values that were pasted in, so audit pasted data.

13.2 Conditional Formatting Basics

Conditional formatting changes how a cell looks when a rule is true. It is found under Home, Conditional Formatting, and the formatting disappears when the rule stops being true.

Rule typeWhat it doesExample
Highlight Cells RulesColours cells that are greater than, equal to, duplicate and so onUnits Sold of 50 or more
Top/Bottom RulesFinds the best or worst valuesTop 5 revenue orders
Data BarsA bar in the cell, longer for bigger valuesCompare revenue at a glance
Color ScalesShades from low to highRevenue heat map
Icon SetsArrows, traffic lights, ticksTarget achievement

Try these on your sales workbook:

  • Select G3:G32, choose Highlight Cells Rules, Greater Than, type 49, and pick a fill. Three orders light up: ORD-010 (60), ORD-013 (50) and ORD-019 (80).

  • Select I3:I32, choose Top/Bottom Rules, Top 10 Items and change 10 to 5. The five biggest orders are ORD-028, ORD-010, ORD-015, ORD-019 and ORD-002.

  • Select A3:A32, choose Highlight Cells Rules, Duplicate Values. Nothing lights up, which confirms every Order ID is unique.

13.3 Colouring a Whole Row with a Formula

Built-in rules colour only the selected cell. To colour the whole row, use a formula rule.

  1. Select A3:J32.

  2. Choose Conditional Formatting, New Rule, Use a formula to determine which cells to format.

  3. Type =$J3="Cancelled".

  4. Click Format, pick a light red fill, and click OK twice.

Rows ORD-007, ORD-017 and ORD-026 turn red. The $ before J locks the column so every cell in the row checks column J, while the row number is free to change. Remember that $J3 is a mixed reference (Chapter 8).

13.4 Managing Rules

  • Conditional Formatting, Manage Rules lists every rule, lets you edit, reorder or delete it, and shows what the rule applies to.

  • Clear Rules removes formatting from the selection or the whole sheet.

  • Too many colours confuse readers. Use two or three, and keep the meaning consistent: for example red always means a problem.

Common mistake: copying and pasting cells over a range with rules. It splits the rule into many fragments. Use Paste Special, Values to keep your rules tidy.

Chapter 13 Summary

  • Data Validation stops bad entries. A drop-down list is the most useful type.

  • Circle Invalid Data finds problems already in the sheet.

  • Conditional formatting highlights what matters, and updates itself as data changes.

  • A formula rule with a locked column colours a whole row.

Practice: Chapter 13

  1. Add a drop-down to Status with the three allowed values.

  2. Highlight every cancelled row in red.

  3. Highlight the top 5 orders by revenue.

  4. Check that Order IDs have no duplicates.

  5. Highlight orders of 50 or more units.

Answers are in Appendix D.

Chapter 14: Charts

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 14 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Why it matters. A manager will read a chart in five seconds and a table in five minutes. A good chart answers one question clearly. A bad one, such as a cluttered 3-D pie, hides the answer.

14.1 Build a Chart in Four Steps

  1. Prepare the data. You need a small, clean summary: labels in the first column and numbers beside them. For revenue by region, use the PivotTable from Chapter 15 or type the five regions and their totals.

  2. Select the data, including the headings.

  3. Insert a chart. On the Insert tab choose a chart type, or click Recommended Charts and let Excel suggest.

  4. Finish it. Add a clear title, remove clutter, and label what matters.

Shortcut: select the data and press Alt + F1 for an instant column chart on the same sheet, or F11 for a chart on its own sheet.

14.2 Choosing the Right Chart

Figure 14.1: Column, line, doughnut and scatter charts. Each answers a different question.

Your questionChartNotes
Which category is bigger?Column or barSort from largest to smallest. Use bars for long labels
How is it changing over time?LinePut time on the horizontal axis
What share does each part hold?Doughnut or pieOnly for about five slices or fewer
Are two measures related?ScatterEach point is one record
Two measures in different unitsComboFor example revenue as columns and growth as a line
Progress against a targetBar with a target markerKeep it simple

14.3 The Parts of a Chart

Click a chart to show the Chart Design and Format tabs, and the three buttons beside it: Chart Elements (+), Chart Styles (brush) and Chart Filters (funnel).

  • Chart title: say what the chart shows. "Lagos and Kano generate 58% of Q1 revenue" beats "Revenue by Region".

  • Axes: the horizontal axis carries categories or time, and the vertical axis carries values.

  • Data labels: put the numbers on the bars so readers do not need gridlines.

  • Legend: needed only when there is more than one series.

  • Gridlines: light grey, or removed once you have data labels.

To change what a chart plots, right-click it and choose Select Data. To switch type, choose Change Chart Type.

14.4 Rules for Honest, Clear Charts

  • Start the value axis of a bar or column chart at zero. Cutting it off exaggerates differences.

  • One message per chart. If you need to say three things, make three charts.

  • Avoid 3-D effects, heavy shadows and rainbow colours.

  • Use one colour for the main series, and a second colour to highlight what matters.

  • Sort categories by value unless they have a natural order, like months.

  • Label units: "NGN million" or "%".

  • Write alt text (right-click, Edit Alt Text) so screen readers can describe the chart.

14.5 Worked Example: Revenue by Region

From the PivotTable, the totals are Lagos 2,145,900, Kano 1,822,800, Port Harcourt 1,129,500, Abuja 965,700 and Ibadan 825,000. Select them, insert a clustered column chart, sort the data largest first, add data labels, delete the legend and the gridlines, and title it "Lagos and Kano generate 58% of Q1 revenue". (2,145,900 plus 1,822,800 is 3,968,700, or 57.6% of 6,888,900.)

For monthly revenue (Jan 2,357,500, Feb 2,375,000, Mar 2,156,400) use a line chart. Notice that the drop in March is clearer when the vertical axis is not crushed from zero to a huge number, so use a sensible axis range on line charts.

14.6 Sparklines and Copying Charts

  • Sparklines are tiny charts inside a cell. Choose Insert, Sparklines, pick a data range and a location. They are ideal beside monthly figures in a table.

  • To use a chart in Word or PowerPoint, click the chart, press Ctrl + C, and paste. Choose Keep Source Formatting and Link Data if it should update with the workbook, or Picture for a fixed image.

Chapter 14 Summary

  • Prepare a small summary first, then select it and insert a chart.

  • Match the chart to the question: columns to compare, lines for time, doughnuts for shares, scatter for relationships.

  • Make the title a message, and remove everything that does not help.

  • Start bar and column axes at zero.

Practice: Chapter 14

  1. Build a column chart of revenue by region, sorted largest first, with data labels.

  2. Build a line chart of monthly revenue.

  3. Build a doughnut chart of revenue share by category. The shares should be Groceries 40%, Electronics 21%, Clothing 21% and Household 18%.

  4. Write a message title for each chart.

  5. Add a sparkline for the three months.

Answers are in Appendix D.

Chapter 15: PivotTables

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 15 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Why it matters. A PivotTable summarises thousands of rows in seconds, with no formulas. It is the tool analysts use most for questions such as "revenue by region and category", and you build it by dragging fields, not by typing.

15.1 Prepare Your Data

A PivotTable needs tidy data:

  • One header row, with a unique, non-blank name above every column.

  • One record per row, and no blank rows or columns inside the data.

  • No merged cells, no subtotal rows, and no mixed data types in a column.

  • Best of all, it is an Excel Table (Ctrl + T), so the PivotTable can grow with the data.

Your Chapter 7 workbook already meets these rules.

15.2 Create a PivotTable

  1. Click any cell in the data.

  2. Choose Insert, PivotTable.

  3. Check the range, and choose New Worksheet. Click OK.

  4. In the PivotTable Fields pane, tick the fields you want, or drag them into the four areas.

Figure 15.1: Region in Rows, Product Category in Columns, and Sum of Revenue in Values.

AreaHoldsExample
RowsGroups down the sideRegion
ColumnsGroups across the topProduct Category
ValuesThe numbers to summariseRevenue (NGN)
FiltersA filter over the whole tableStatus

The table in the figure shows Lagos is the biggest region at 2,145,900, and that Kano's Groceries (1,290,000) is the single biggest region and category cell.

15.3 Change the Calculation

Values are added up by default. To change that, right-click a value and choose Summarize Values By, or open Value Field Settings.

OptionUse it toExample
SumAdd upRevenue by region
CountCount recordsOrders per region (Lagos 10, the other four regions 5 each)
AverageTypical valueAverage order size
Max / MinExtremesLargest order per rep

Show Values As turns numbers into shares. Choose % of Grand Total and the regions read Lagos 31.1%, Kano 26.5%, Port Harcourt 16.4%, Abuja 14.0% and Ibadan 12.0%.

Right-click a number and choose Number Format to show thousands separators. Formatting the cells directly is lost when the PivotTable changes.

15.4 Group, Filter and Slice

  • Group dates: put Order Date in Rows, right-click a date and choose Group, Months. You get January 2,357,500, February 2,375,000 and March 2,156,400.

  • Report filter: drag Status to Filters and pick Completed. The grand total becomes 4,874,400.

  • Slicers: on the PivotTable Analyze tab choose Insert Slicer, tick Status, and click buttons to filter. Slicers are friendly for people who do not use PivotTables.

  • Sort: right-click a value, then Sort, Largest to Smallest.

  • Double-click any value to see the underlying rows. It is a quick way to check where a number comes from.

15.5 Refresh and PivotCharts

A PivotTable does not update automatically when the data changes. After editing the source, right-click the PivotTable and choose Refresh, or press Alt + F5. If you added new rows outside an Excel Table, change the source under PivotTable Analyze, Change Data Source.

To chart a PivotTable, click inside it and choose Insert, PivotChart. The chart follows the table, and filters apply to both.

Common mistakes: a blank header, which gives the error "field name is not valid"; numbers stored as text, which get counted instead of summed; typing over a PivotTable cell, which is not allowed. Change the fields, not the cells.

Chapter 15 Summary

  • A PivotTable needs tidy data with one header row.

  • Drag fields into Rows, Columns, Values and Filters.

  • Change Sum to Count or Average, or show values as a percentage.

  • Group dates, add slicers, and refresh after the data changes.

Practice: Chapter 15

  1. Build a PivotTable of revenue by Sales Rep. Who is top?

  2. Show the number of orders per region.

  3. Which product category has the highest revenue?

  4. Filter to Completed orders. What is the grand total?

  5. Group by month and report the three monthly totals.

Chapter 16: Printing, Sharing and Protecting

Practise this chapter: take the Chapter 16 quiz in the Excel Handbook Lab.

Why it matters. Your work is only useful once someone else can read it. A report that prints across five pages, a file that gets overwritten, or a formula that a colleague deletes by accident can cost you your credibility. This chapter makes your workbook ready for the real world.

16.1 Prepare to Print

Open the Page Layout tab.

SettingWhereAdvice
OrientationPage Layout, OrientationLandscape for wide tables
MarginsPage Layout, MarginsNarrow when a table is wide
Print AreaSelect the range, Page Layout, Print Area, Set Print AreaPrints only what you choose
Print TitlesPage Layout, Print TitlesRepeats the header row on every page
Scale to FitWidth: 1 page, Height: AutomaticStops columns spilling onto extra pages
Page breaksView, Page Break PreviewDrag the blue lines to control breaks

For the sales sheet, open Print Titles and set Rows to repeat at top to $2:$2 so the column headings appear on every page.

16.2 Headers, Footers and Print Preview

  • Choose Insert, Header & Footer to add a page number, the file name and the date. A footer such as "Page 1 of 3" helps readers keep the pages in order.

  • Press Ctrl + P to open Print Preview. Check every page before printing. Use the arrows at the bottom to move through pages.

  • To print only part of a sheet, select it and choose Print Selection in the settings.

16.3 Save as PDF

A PDF keeps the layout exactly as you set it and cannot be edited by accident. Choose File, Save As (or Export), pick PDF as the type, and click Options to publish only the selection or active sheet. Always open the PDF afterwards to check it.

16.4 Sharing a Workbook

MethodWhen to useWatch out for
Email attachmentOne-off reviewsVersions multiply quickly
Share via OneDriveSeveral people edit the same fileEveryone sees changes live
PDFFinal reportNo editing possible
CSVSend raw data to another systemLoses formatting and multiple sheets

Other good sharing habits:

  • Name files clearly and with a version, such as Zenith_Q1_Sales_2024_v2.xlsx. Never use "final_final".

  • Use Review, New Comment to ask a question about a cell, and New Note for a permanent remark.

  • With files on OneDrive, File, Info, Version History lets you restore earlier versions.

  • Before sending outside your team, remove personal data. Choose File, Info, Check for Issues, Inspect Document.

16.5 Protecting Your Work

  • Protect Sheet (Review, Protect Sheet) stops people changing locked cells. Cells are locked by default, but the lock only works once the sheet is protected.

  • To let people edit certain cells, unlock them first: select them, press Ctrl + 1, open Protection and untick Locked. Then protect the sheet.

  • Protect Workbook Structure stops people adding, deleting or moving sheets.

  • Mark as Final is a polite signal that the file is complete.

Warning: if you set a password and forget it, Excel cannot recover it. Keep passwords somewhere safe. Sheet protection is also meant to prevent accidents, not to keep secrets, so never rely on it for confidential data. Use File, Info, Protect Workbook, Encrypt with Password for that, and share the password through a separate channel.

16.6 File Types

TypeExtensionUse
Workbook.xlsxNormal file, no macros
Macro-enabled.xlsmContains macros
Template.xltxA reusable starting point
CSV.csvPlain data, one sheet
PDF.pdfFinal, read-only output

Back up regularly. Turn on AutoSave if the file is on OneDrive, and keep a copy before large changes. Excel can also recover unsaved work under File, Info, Manage Workbook.

Chapter 16 Summary

  • Set orientation, print titles and scale-to-fit before you print.

  • Check Print Preview, and save a PDF for final reports.

  • Name files with versions, and inspect files before sharing.

  • Unlock input cells, then protect the sheet. Never lose the password.

Practice: Chapter 16

  1. Set the sales sheet to landscape, one page wide, with the header row repeating on each page.

  2. Add a footer showing the page number and file name.

  3. Open Print Preview and check the page count.

  4. Save the sheet as a PDF and open it.

  5. Unlock the Status column, protect the sheet, and test that other cells cannot be changed.

There is a self-check list in Appendix D.

Chapter 17: Capstone Project

Practise this chapter: finish with the mixed challenge in the Excel Handbook Lab.

This project brings Chapters 1 to 16 together. You will turn the Q1 sales workbook into a one-sheet management report, the kind of work a junior analyst is asked for in the first month of a job.

17.1 The Brief

The Head of Sales at Zenith Consumer Goods Limited asks: "Give me one page that shows how Q1 went, who is performing, and what needs attention. I have five minutes before the meeting."

17.2 Steps

  1. Clean and check (Ch 4, 10, 12). Confirm every date is a real date, there are no extra spaces, and Revenue is a formula. Check that revenue totals 6,888,900.

  2. Add helper columns (Ch 9, 10). Add Month (=TEXT(B3,"mmm")), Order Size (Large, Medium or Small, from Chapter 9) and Rep Target (XLOOKUP, Chapter 11).

  3. Add controls (Ch 13). Add a Status drop-down, and shade cancelled rows red.

  4. Create a Summary sheet with these KPIs (Ch 8, 9). Use formulas, not typed numbers:

KPIFormula ideaExpected value
Total revenueSUM6,888,900
Completed revenueSUMIF on Status4,874,400
Pending revenueSUMIF on Status1,540,000 (5 orders)
Cancelled revenueSUMIF on Status474,500 (3 orders)
Average orderAVERAGE229,630
Number of ordersCOUNTA30

  1. Add a rep scorecard (Ch 11). For each rep show target, revenue and achievement. Sort it largest first. Funke Adeleke should lead at 214.4%.

  2. Add a PivotTable (Ch 15) of revenue by region and category, and refresh it.

  3. Add two charts (Ch 14): revenue by region (columns) and monthly revenue (line), each with a message title.

  4. Write three insights in cells under the charts. Examples of what the data supports:

    • Lagos and Kano generated 57.6% of Q1 revenue.

    • Groceries are 40.0% of revenue, and Kano's Groceries alone are 1,290,000.

    • March revenue fell 9.2% from February, and 1,540,000 is still pending.

  5. Print-ready (Ch 16). Set landscape, fit to one page, add a footer, and save a PDF named Zenith_Q1_Sales_Report.pdf.

  6. Protect. Protect the Summary sheet so formulas cannot be overwritten.

17.3 Self-Marking Checklist

SkillDone?
All KPI figures match the expected values
Every figure is a formula or a PivotTable, nothing typed
Dates, text and number formats are consistent
Both charts have message titles and labelled units
The scorecard uses a lookup and a percentage format
Cancelled rows are highlighted, Status has a drop-down
The report prints on one page and exports to PDF
The sheet is protected, and you remember the password

If you tick all eight, you are ready for the next stage of the programme.

17.4 Reflection

  1. Which step took longest, and what would make it faster next time?

  2. Which function from Part 2 will you use most at work?

  3. Which error did you meet, and how did you fix it?

  4. What is one question your manager might ask that this report cannot yet answer?

Reflection Questions: Model Answers

  1. True dates are stored as numbers, so they right-align. Text dates left-align and will not sort chronologically or filter by month.

  2. Absolute references would lock every row to row 2, so each Revenue cell would repeat ORD-001's result.

  3. Excel sorts by the first level, then by the second only within ties. Reversing them would group by revenue first and make region groupings meaningless.

  4. Open the Product Category filter and tick both Electronics and Clothing. Ticking several values in one column is an OR.

  5. Examples: a revenue-by-region summary, a PivotTable, conditional formatting on Cancelled orders, and data validation on Status.

Appendix E: Glossary

TermMeaning
Absolute referenceA cell reference locked with dollar signs so it does not change when copied
Active cellThe selected cell, with the green border, that receives what you type
ArgumentA value or range you give to a function, inside its brackets
AutoFillDragging the Fill Handle to copy or extend a pattern
AutoSumA button (Alt + =) that writes a SUM formula for you
CellOne box where a row and a column meet
Cell addressColumn letter plus row number, such as C5
ChartA picture of numbers, such as a column or line chart
Conditional formattingFormatting that applies automatically when a rule is true
CSVA plain text file of data separated by commas
Data validationRules that limit what can be typed into a cell
DatasetA table of records: one row per record and one column per field
Fill HandleThe small square at the bottom-right of the active cell
FilterHides rows that do not match your criteria without deleting them
Flash FillFills a column by recognising the pattern in your examples (Ctrl + E)
FormulaAn instruction starting with = that calculates a result
Formula BarThe bar that shows what a cell really contains
Freeze PanesKeeps rows or columns visible while you scroll
FunctionA ready-made formula, such as SUM or IF
Name BoxThe box at the left of the Formula Bar showing the active cell's address
PivotTableAn interactive summary table built by dragging fields
RangeA group of cells, such as A1:A10
RecordOne row of data, such as a single order
Relative referenceA reference that shifts when a formula is copied
RibbonThe band of tabs, groups and commands at the top of the window
SlicerA set of buttons that filters a table or PivotTable
SortReorder rows by the values in one or more columns
Status BarThe bar at the bottom showing the sum, average and count of a selection
TableA range converted with Ctrl + T that has filters and grows automatically
Volatile functionA function such as TODAY that recalculates every time the workbook opens
WildcardA symbol in a criterion, such as * for any text
WorkbookAn Excel file
WorksheetOne page (tab) inside a workbook
